interview.name: Change requests and extra work
interview.description: How Brightline handles client requests for extra or changed work.

turns.question: When a client asks for something new in the middle of a project, what usually happens next? A recent example helps.
suggestedAnswers: We usually just build it if it's small

learned.businessGoal: Get paid for every piece of extra work a client asks for
learned.trigger: A client asks for something that is not in the statement of work, usually in the shared Slack channel

steps.name: Client asks for extra work
steps.description: The client posts a request in the shared Slack channel, for example a third dashboard.

turns.question: Who decides whether that extra work is billable, and how do they decide?
suggestedAnswers: I decide, mostly by gut feel
Anything over a day gets a change order

decisions: Extra work estimated above one day needs a written change order before it starts
approvals: The owner approves the price on every change order

steps.name: Estimate the request
steps.description: The project lead sizes the request against the statement of work.
steps.decision: Is this more than a day of work?

turns.question: Where does the client's approval get recorded: email, Slack, a signed change order, or somewhere else?

exceptions: Small fixes under two hours are done without a change order

steps.name: Client approves the change order
steps.description: The client replies by email or in Slack to approve the change order.

turns.question: How does an approved change order make it onto the invoice? Walk me through the last one.
suggestedAnswers: I add it to the next milestone invoice

learned.frequency: Two or three extra requests a month across active projects
bottlenecks: Approved extras are added to the next milestone invoice from memory, so some are forgotten
Work often starts before the change order is approved

steps.name: Add the change order to the next invoice
steps.description: The owner adds the approved extra to the next milestone invoice in QuickBooks.

turns.question: Thinking about the last six months, where did money slip through? Any extra work you never billed?
suggestedAnswers: One big one: a third dashboard

learned.desiredOutcome: Every approved extra appears on an invoice in the same month it was approved
bottlenecks: Requests arrive in Slack where nobody checks them against the contract
automationOpportunities: Flag a Slack request that matches a contract exclusion
Draft the change order from the request and the contract

interview.closing: Thanks, that's clear. Knov now knows that extra work over a day needs a written change order, that approvals arrive by email or Slack, and that approved extras are added to the next milestone invoice from memory. Review what it learned and correct anything that's off.

interview.name: Proposals and follow-ups
interview.description: The promises Kestrel makes to clients and how they are tracked.

turns.question: When you promise a client a proposal or a follow-up, where does that promise get written down?

steps.name: Promise a proposal

turns.question: How do you decide the date you promise, and how often does it hold?
suggestedAnswers: Usually a week; it holds about half the time

learned.frequency: Three or four proposals a month

turns.question: Who writes the proposal, with what, and what does it need before it can go out?
suggestedAnswers: I write it in Google Docs from a template

steps.name: Draft the proposal
steps.description: The associate drafts the proposal in Google Docs from the template and workshop notes.

steps.name: Review and send
steps.description: The owner reviews the pricing and sends the proposal PDF to the client.

approvals: The owner approves pricing before any proposal is sent

turns.question: What happens after you send it? Is there a follow-up rhythm if the client goes quiet?
suggestedAnswers: I follow up after a week

steps.name: Follow up on the proposal
steps.description: The owner emails a short follow-up one week after sending.

exceptions: Existing clients get a call instead of a written proposal

turns.question: Think of a deal you lost or nearly lost because a proposal was late. What happened?
suggestedAnswers: A board meeting came and went
The client went with someone faster

learned.desiredOutcome: No proposal goes out later than promised, and every sent proposal gets a follow-up
bottlenecks: Promised dates live only in email threads, so there is nothing to remind the owner
automationOpportunities: Pull promised dates out of sent emails and show which ones are overdue
Draft the follow-up email from the original promise

interview.closing: Thanks. Knov now knows that proposals are promised a week out by email, drafted in Google Docs, and reviewed by the owner, and that promised dates are tracked nowhere but the thread. Review what it learned and correct anything that's off.
